query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Short-range chemical order (SRO) within multi-component concentrated alloys modifies local planar fault energies and dislocation pathways, primarily governing their strength and failure by altering dislocation slip, twinning, and fault evolution.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-component concentrated alloy in a near-equiatomic composition, processed to an as-cast or solution-annealed state with minimal or moderate short-range order.
generation.intervention: Vary the solution-annealing temperature and cooling rate to systematically tune the degree of local short-range order, then evaluate how these changes affect mechanical response and microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: Room to moderate temperatures (up to ~0.5Tm) and quasi-static loading rates to capture dislocation-mediated plasticity and any associated fault or twinning phenomena.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical clustering and short-range ordering that alter stacking fault energies and dislocation–fault interactions.
generation.mechanism: Increased SRO raises local energy barriers for dislocation motion and faulting, promoting planar slip and suppressing cross-slip and twinning or transformations, thereby enhancing strength and altering failure pathways.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with higher SRO will exhibit moderately increased yield strength (on the order of tens of percent above baseline), more planar dislocation arrangements, and reduced twinning or transformations compared to alloys with minimal SRO.
generation.baseline: The baseline is an alloy variant that has undergone heat treatment to minimize SRO, facilitating relatively lower yield strength, more pronounced cross-slip, and higher twinning activity.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis primarily applies to FCC-based multi-component alloys with substantial compositional disorder and not necessarily to high-temperature BCC alloys or systems with significantly different stacking-fault energy regimes.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work implicates SRO in strengthening, the precise magnitude of strength increase and specific SRO features driving deformation remain uncertain and may vary with alloy composition and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce alloy batches with identical compositions but subject them to varied solution-annealing times and cooling rates to achieve distinct SRO levels (confirmed by diffraction and atom probe). Perform tensile/compressive tests under matching strain rates and temperatures. Employ high-resolution microscopy or in situ methods to observe dislocation arrangements and fault formation, correlating microstructure with mechanical response.
measurements: Atom probe tomography or diffraction to quantify short-range order
Mechanical testing (yield stress, plastic flow stress, strain hardening, fracture modes)
Electron microscopy/in situ techniques to track dislocation slip, twin formation, and fault bounding
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If modifications in SRO do not produce systematic changes in measured fault energies, dislocation structures, or mechanical properties under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis that short-range chemical order is the primary governing factor of strength and failure behavior is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceComplex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with multi elements in equiatomic ratios are exotic alloys but what governs their strength is currently not clearly understood. This work has proven the prime origin of strength in CCAs as arising from the fluctuations (not the averaged value) of the shear-fault energy, which is an important feature of CCAs unrecognized beforehand. Through identification of the local hard atomic motifs far beyond the traditional concept of the globally averaged short-range ordering parameters, this work has unfolded the physical basis of strength in CCAs and provides important clues for designing high-strength CCAs by focusing on the alloy composition to produce large fault-energy fluctuations. Local chemical short-range ordering (SRO) and spatial fluctuations of planar fault energy are important features of multi-element and metastable complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Arising from them, dislocations in such alloys are distinctively wavy in both static and migrating conditions; yet, such effects on strength have remained unknown. High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys for the design of strong and ductile materials. AbstractMulti–principal element alloys (MPEAs) containing three or more components in high concentrations render a tunable chemical short-range order (SRO). Leveraging large-scale atomistic simulations, we probe the limit of Hall-Petch strengthening and deformation mechanisms in a model CrCoNi alloy and unravel chemical ordering effects. The presence of SRO appreciably increases the maximum strength and lowers the propensity for faulting and structure transformation, accompanied by intensification of planar slip and strain localization. Deformation grains exhibit notably different microstructures and dislocation patterns that prominently depend on their crystallographic orientation and the number of active slip planes. Grain of single-planar slip attains the highest volume fraction of deformation-induced structure transformation, and grain with double-slip planes develops the densest dislocation network. These results advancing the fundamental understanding of deformation mechanisms and dislocation patterning in MPEAs suggest a mechanistic strategy for tuning mechanical behavior through simultaneously tailoring grain texture and local chemical order. decision.trend: Early work focused on using theory-driven design to identify suitable high-entropy and complex concentrated alloys with strong solid-solution strengthening and distinct local atomic environments. Subsequent studies demonstrated that short-range or local chemical order can form even in nominally ‘disordered’ multi-principal element alloys, which alters planar fault energies and dislocation pathways to improve strength and influence deformation modes. Later investigations exploited grain boundary engineering—exploring how grain boundaries serve as nucleation sites for twins or dislocations—and revealed that heterogeneous lattice strain fields, mechanical twinning, and nanoscale structural transformations also contribute significantly to strength and ductility. Most recent efforts emphasize how local fault-energy fluctuations and defect (e.g., stacking fault or dislocation) interactions with short-range ordering can dominate mechanical responses under various loading conditions, highlighting the interplay of chemistry, defects, and microstructure in shaping mechanical strength, ductility, and failure mechanisms.
decision.unsolved: Despite this growing emphasis on local chemical order and structural heterogeneities, a clear, experimentally verified framework linking the precise nature, distribution, and evolution of short-range order and atomic-level inhomogeneities to macroscopic flow strength and strain-hardening response remains elusive. Challenges include quantitatively measuring and controlling the degree of local ordering across length scales, and correlating these local states with specific defect interactions under different processing histories and test conditions.
decision.lever: Vary solution-annealing conditions and cooling rates to tune short-range order, then correlate local chemical ordering (via in situ diffraction and atom probe tomography) with dislocation activities observed by high-resolution microscopy and advanced simulations. Compare mechanical responses and corresponding dislocation mechanisms under these targeted thermal histories.
decision.why: This approach directly tests whether the hypothesized controlling role of short-range chemical fluctuations and associated fault-energy barriers in defining strength, dislocation motion, and twinning/faulting propensities holds under systematic changes in thermal history and local order, providing a rigorous and quantitative link between structure, composition, and mechanical response.
